cols: Billions of metric tons of carbon per year
rows: Added: combustion of fossil fuels and cement making
Removed: taken up by the ocean
Removed: taken up by plants and soils on land

carbon-cycle-s2.title: Carbon dioxide over two years at one station

plot.label: Line graph of monthly carbon dioxide in the air at a northern station over two years, rising each year with a yearly up-and-down cycle, invented data

items.q: Which process moves carbon from the atmosphere into living things?
options: Photosynthesis
Cellular respiration
Combustion
Decomposition

why.correct: Plants, algae and some bacteria take in CO2 and build it into sugars during photosynthesis.
options: Right: photosynthesis takes CO2 out of the air.
Respiration releases CO2 to the air.
Combustion releases CO2 to the air.
Decomposition releases CO2 as decomposers respire.

items.q: Which reservoir holds by far the most carbon on Earth?
options: Sedimentary rock
The atmosphere
Living plants and animals
Soil and dead matter

why.correct: Most of Earth’s carbon is locked in sedimentary rock such as limestone and in ocean sediments, where it stays for millions of years.
options: Right: rock and sediments are the largest, slowest reservoir.
The atmosphere is a small reservoir compared with rocks and the ocean.
Living things hold far less than rocks or the ocean.
Soil holds more than the air, but far less than rock and sediment.

items.q: Why does burning fossil fuels increase the CO2 in the atmosphere so much faster than natural processes remove it?
options: It releases in decades carbon buried over millions of years.
It turns the oxygen in the air directly into carbon dioxide.
It stops photosynthesis in the forests near the fuel.
It releases methane, which then hardens into rock.

why.correct: Fossil fuels are ancient carbon that the slow part of the cycle buried. Combustion releases it far faster than photosynthesis, the ocean and sedimentation can take it back up.
options: Right: slow-cycle carbon is released at a fast-cycle rate.
Combustion joins carbon from the fuel with oxygen; the carbon comes from the fuel.
Photosynthesis continues; it is just slower than the release.
Methane does not turn into rock.

items.q: A forest takes in more carbon by photosynthesis each year than it releases. What is the forest?
options: A carbon sink
A carbon source
A fossil fuel reservoir
A flux of zero

why.correct: A sink takes in more carbon than it releases, so carbon builds up in it.
options: Right: net uptake makes it a sink.
A source releases more than it takes in.
Living forests are not fossil fuel reservoirs.
The flux into the forest is larger than the flux out, so the net flux is not zero.

items.q: In a carbon cycle diagram, which arrow represents decomposition?
options: Dead matter in the soil to the air
Atmosphere to plants and algae
Ocean to sedimentary rock
Fossil fuels to the atmosphere

why.correct: Decomposers break down dead matter and release its carbon to the air as CO2 by respiration (or as methane where oxygen is scarce).
options: Right: decomposers return carbon in dead matter to the air.
That arrow is photosynthesis.
That arrow is sedimentation.
That arrow is combustion.

items.q: Plant matter in wet, oxygen-poor soil (such as a swamp) breaks down slowly and releases methane rather than mostly CO2. Why?
options: Without oxygen, some microbes decompose matter in ways that release methane.
The water in the swamp turns the carbon dioxide into methane.
Plants in swamps do not carry out photosynthesis, so methane builds up.
Swamps lack decomposers, so the dead matter turns into methane by itself.

why.correct: Where oxygen is scarce, some microbes break down dead matter without oxygen and release methane, and decomposition is slower, so dead matter piles up.
options: Right: oxygen-free decomposition releases methane.
Water does not convert CO2 to methane.
Swamp plants do photosynthesize.
Decomposers are present; they just work differently and more slowly.

items.q: Which change would move the most carbon from a fast reservoir to the atmosphere in a single year?
options: Burning a large forest
Shells settling on the ocean floor
Limestone forming over many years
A tree growing a crop of new leaves

why.correct: Burning releases the carbon stored in the trees as CO2 within days. Shells settling and rock forming remove carbon from the air slowly, and growth takes carbon in.
options: Right: combustion of plant matter releases its carbon quickly.
Sedimentation stores carbon; it does not release it.
Rock formation stores carbon over long times.
Growth takes carbon out of the air.

items.q: A farmer drains a peat-rich swamp to grow crops. Explain how this affects atmospheric CO2.

why.correct: Draining lets oxygen in, so decomposers break down the stored dead matter faster and release CO2.

specific.frame: Draining lets ___ into the soil, so decomposers break down stored dead matter ___, which ___ the CO2 in the atmosphere.

cause.label: What gets in
options: oxygen
nitrogen
sunlight

why.1: The key change for decomposers is oxygen, which speeds up their respiration.
why.2: Light does not reach far into soil and is not what speeds decomposition.

rate.label: Rate
options: faster
more slowly

why.1: More oxygen speeds decomposition; waterlogging is what slowed it.

effect.label: Effect on CO2
options: increases
decreases

why.1: Faster decomposition releases stored carbon as CO2, so it rises.

specific.model: Draining lets oxygen into the swamp soil, so decomposers break down the stored dead matter faster, which increases the CO2 in the atmosphere.

items.q: How does the ocean take up carbon from the atmosphere?
options: CO2 dissolves at the surface, and algae use it.
Fish at the surface breathe in CO2 from the air.
Breaking waves turn the CO2 into oxygen gas.
Seawater pushes CO2 away, so the ocean just releases it.

why.correct: CO2 dissolves at the sea surface, and algae near the surface build it into sugars; some carbon sinks to deep water and sediments.
options: Right: dissolving plus photosynthesis by algae.
Fish take in oxygen from water and release CO2.
Waves mix water but do not change CO2 into oxygen.
The ocean both takes in and releases CO2; overall it takes in more today.

items.q: How much carbon do human activities add to the atmosphere in the year shown? Give the total with its scale word and unit, such as 2.5 billion metric tons.

why.correct: $9.7 + 1.1 = 10.8$ billion metric tons of carbon ($1.08 \times 10^{10}$ metric tons).

mistakes.why: You added the two removals (2.9 + 3.2). The question asks what is added: 9.7 + 1.1.
Keep the scale word: the table is in billions, so write billion (or × 10^9) with the number.

items.q: How much of the added carbon stays in the atmosphere that year? Subtract both removals from the total added, and give the answer with its scale word and unit.

why.correct: Added: $9.7 + 1.1 = 10.8$. Removed: $2.9 + 3.2 = 6.1$. Left in the air: $10.8 - 6.1 = 4.7$ billion metric tons ($4.7 \times 10^{9}$ metric tons).

mistakes.why: You subtracted only the ocean (10.8 - 2.9). Land plants and soils remove carbon too: subtract both.
You left out the forest clearing. The total added is 9.7 + 1.1 = 10.8.
Keep the scale word: the table is in billions, so write billion (or × 10^9) with the number.

items.q: Which conclusion do the data support?
options: Sinks remove a bit over half of the added carbon.
The ocean removes more carbon than plants and soils on land do.
Natural sinks remove the whole amount of carbon people add.
Clearing forests adds more carbon than burning fossil fuels does.

why.correct: Removed $2.9 + 3.2 = 6.1$ of $10.8$ added, a bit more than half (about 56%). The rest stays in the air.
options: Right: 6.1 of 10.8 is a little over half.
Land (3.2) removes more than the ocean (2.9).
6.1 is less than 10.8, so some carbon stays in the air.
Forest clearing (1.1) adds far less than fossil fuels (9.7).

items.q: Which two patterns does the graph show?
options: A yearly rise, with a peak in spring and a dip in late summer
A steady fall from one year to the next, with no seasonal cycle
A rise each summer and a fall each winter, with no yearly trend
No change over the two years shown on the graph

why.correct: Each year ends higher (about 419 to 421.5 ppm in December), and within each year CO2 is highest around May and lowest around September.
options: Right: an upward trend plus a yearly cycle.
The values rise from year 1 to year 2.
The dips come in late summer, not the peaks.
Year 2 is about 2 to 3 ppm higher than year 1.

items.q: Why does CO2 fall from about May to September at a northern station?
options: Northern plants photosynthesize more in summer.
People burn more fossil fuels in the summer months.
Decomposition of dead leaves speeds up in summer.
The ocean releases more CO2 during the summer.

why.correct: Most land is in the Northern Hemisphere. In its growing season, photosynthesis takes in more CO2 than respiration and decomposition release, so CO2 falls.
options: Right: summer photosynthesis draws CO2 down.
More burning would raise CO2, not lower it.
More decomposition would raise CO2.
Releasing CO2 would raise it.

items.q: By how much did CO2 change from month 1 (418 ppm) to month 13 (420.5 ppm)?

mistakes.why: Subtract the old value from the new: 420.5 - 418, so the change is +2.5 ppm.

items.q: A student predicted that CO2 would be highest in summer, when people run air conditioners. Do the data support the prediction?
options: No: CO2 is lowest in late summer and highest in spring.
Yes: CO2 peaks in July and August of each year.
Yes: CO2 rises steadily through each summer.
No: CO2 stays the same from month to month.

why.correct: The highest values are in May (months 5 and 17) and the lowest in September (months 9 and 21), so the prediction is not supported.
options: Right: the low point is in late summer.
Months 7 and 8 (and 19 and 20) are falling, not peaking.
CO2 falls through summer in the graph.
CO2 changes by several ppm within each year.

items.q: Over millions of years, the shells of tiny sea organisms pile up on the ocean floor and harden into limestone. What does this do to carbon?
options: It stores carbon in rock for a long time.
It releases the carbon to the air in a few days.
It moves the carbon into the soil of forests.
It turns the carbon into another element.

why.correct: Sedimentation locks carbon away in sedimentary rock, the slowest, largest reservoir.
options: Right: sedimentation makes a long-term carbon store.
Rock formation is slow and stores carbon.
The carbon stays on the ocean floor, not in forest soil.
Carbon does not turn into another element.
